section_path_text: What is going on in the tanker market?
text:
Shipowners typically look forward to the winter. As the weather gets colder, the tanker market starts to heat up. There are a variety of factors that contribute to this seasonal improvement in the markets. Colder weather in the northern hemisphere boosts energy demand, while winter storms in the north Atlantic, ice in the Baltic and fog in the Black sea reduce fleet productivity in the winter months. As can be seen in the chart of VLCC rates (which is normally fairly representative of all tanker markets), in a "normal" year, the first and in particular the fourth quarter show the highest earnings. As the fourth quarter of 2017 started, it appeared to follow the normal seasonal pattern, but rather than strengthening through November and December, rates plateaued and turned down towards the end of the year and remained depressed into the new year. What caused this counter seasonal slump in tanker rates, and (how long) will it last?
The first area to examine in more detail is tanker demand. According to the IEA, global oil demand in Q4 2017 was a robust 98.3 mb/d, the same level as in Q3 and 1.3 mb/d higher than in Q4 2016. One year later, this number was down to an estimated 24.5 mb/d, a reduction of 1.1 mb/d. So, while global oil demand was up 1.3%, Middle East OPEC production was down 4.3%.
If Middle East OPEC has reduced production (and exports), but oil demand remains strong, where do refiners source the additional crude from? text:
Over the last couple of years, two topics have dominated the oil (and by extension the tanker) markets: OPEC production, or the lack thereof and U.S. shale output. Judging by the amount of ink that is used to discuss these popular themes, one may think that not much is happening in the rest of the world, i.e. the non- OPEC producers outside of the U.S. that are not part of the OPEC/non-OPEC production agreement. That is not entirely true. By the end of 2017, total world oil production reached an estimated 97.8 mb/d. OPEC countries represented roughly 40% of total production. The U.S. is the largest non-OPEC producer with an output of 13.6 m/d (13.9% market share). The 11 non- OPEC producers that participate in the OPEC cuts represent another 19% of global output. Some of these changes could have a material impact on the shipping markets.

section_path: The impact of the Renewable Fuel Standard on U.S. refiners
section_path_text: The impact of the Renewable Fuel Standard on U.S. refiners
text:
Last weekend, Philadelphia Energy Solutions (PES), the largest oil refinery on the U.S. East Coast, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection. PES operates two domestic refineries in Philadelphia with a combined processing capacity of 335,000 barrels per day (b/d). The refinery complex can trace its roots back to 1866, one year after the end of the Civil War, when Atlantic Petroleum Company established its operation at Point Breeze. Atlantic installed its first petroleum refining units in 1870 and changed its name to Atlantic Refining Company. In 2012, PES emerged from a joint venture between private equity firm The Carlyle Group LP and Sunoco Inc., which was bought that year by Energy Transfer Partners LP. What caused the problems at the refiner? PES has pointed to the cost associated with the Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS) as a key driver for its financial troubles. According to PES, the independent refiner spent more than $800 million on Renewable Identification Numbers (RINs) since 2012 to comply with the RFS. What is the background of this government program and why is it so controversial?
The Renewable Fuel Standard was created with the Energy Policy Act of 2005 and was expanded and extended by the Energy Independence and Security Act of 2007. The RFS requires renewable fuel to be blended into transportation fuel in increasing amounts each year, escalating to 36 billion gallons in 2022 (the volumes for 2017 were 25 billion gallons). The original objective of the program was to stimulate the production of renewable fuels to reduce U.S. dependence on foreign oil. In 2006, the U.S. imported more than 60% of its domestic oil requirements. Due to the shale oil boom and the corresponding growth in U.S. production, our dependence on foreign oil has been reduced to some 20% in 2017. Although the changes in U.S. production have increased the discussion about the future of the RFS, the program is still there and it has important implications for refiners, due to the high cost of RINs.
How does it work? The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) administers the RFS program and establishes the volume requirements for each category. The EPA tracks compliance through the Renewable Identification Number (RIN) system. Every time a gallon of ethanol is shipped from a production facility, a RIN is produced.

section_path: The impact of the Renewable Fuel Standard on U.S. refiners

text:
future of the RFS, the program is still there and it has important implications for refiners, due to the high cost of RINs.
How does it work? The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) administers the RFS program and establishes the volume requirements for each category. The EPA tracks compliance through the Renewable Identification Number (RIN) system. Every time a gallon of ethanol is shipped from a production facility, a RIN is produced. This RIN has value and is theoretically included in the price of ethanol when it is sold by the ethanol producer. When the ethanol is purchased by a marketer for example, and blended into gasoline, the RIN is separated and can be sold. Entities regulated by RFS include oil refiners and gasoline and diesel importers. The volumes required of each obligated party are based on a percentage of its petroleum product sales. Obligated parties can meet their renewable volume obligations (RVOs) by either selling required biofuel volumes or purchasing RINs from parties that exceed their requirements. However, the volatility and unpredictability of RIN prices can create a substantial financial burden for merchant-model refiners that don't blend their own fuels.
Not surprisingly, there has been significant political back and forth on this subject, with farm-states (where most of the corn-based ethanol and soy- based bio-diesel is produced) pitted against the oil-states (where most of the refiners are based). So far, no changes to the RFS have been implemented, a significant win for the politicians representing the Midwest. The RFS program is very important for corn farmers: the U.S. Department of Agriculture estimates that some 38% of the U.S. corn crop is destined for ethanol plants.
It is unclear whether the bankruptcy filing of PES will have an impact on the debate. Senators Pat Toomey of Pennsylvania and Ted Cruz of Texas have been working on a number of legislative "fixes" that may offer a compromise: 1) Allow exported biofuels to count towards the refiners RIN quotas and/or 2) Require the EPA to sell "fixed price waiver credits" to refiners. Proposals like this, which reduce compliance cost for independent refiners and keep farmers in business may now have a better chance of being adopted.

section_path: Increased demolition is needed to rebalance the market
section_path_text: Increased demolition is needed to rebalance the market
text:
The tanker market has started 2018 in the doldrums. One of the main reasons for the depressed rate environment is the oversupply of existing tonnage. On top of that, there are still a significant number of newbuilding deliveries scheduled this year for all the major vessel segments and because OPEC has vowed to keep its production cuts in place (at least through June), ton-mile demand growth may be limited. That is why many tanker market observers are looking at demolition as a key driver to rebalance the market and restore health to the freight market. The argument is that as tanker earnings regularly dip below operating expenses and more and more charterers discriminate against older (>15 years) vessels, demolition starts to look more attractive, especially with scrap prices on the rise. The looming regulation changes with respect to Ballast Water Treatment Systems and the Sulphur content of bunker fuels and their associated investments also play a role. What do we think that the practical impact will be of scrapping in the short to medium term?
Back in 1789, Benjamin Franklin said that in this world nothing is certain, except death and taxes. In shipping, many companies shield themselves from most taxes, but the other certainty remains: every ship will eventually be scrapped, typically somewhere between 20 and 25 years old. The scrap age of tankers is heavily influenced by the state of the freight market. During the very challenging tanker market of 1980-1986, VLCCs were scrapped at an average age of 11 years, but in the 2003- 2008 super cycle, the average scrapping age for that vessel class reached a high of 29 years (in 2007). Since the boom-bust cycle is most pronounced in the large tanker market, the average scrapping age of VLCCs tends to be more volatile than that for smaller tankers. The annual average scrapping age of smaller product carriers, for example, has never fallen below 20 years and has typically been between 25 and 30 years. So, while there may be some merit in looking at the VLCC fleet of 16 years old and older (116 vessels, 16% of the total fleet), it is rather meaningless to look at product carriers in this age bracket. For product carriers, 20+ or 25+ years old may be a better target to determine the pool of scrapping candidates.

section_title: (When) will the tanker market improve?
section_path: (When) will the tanker market improve?
section_path_text: (When) will the tanker market improve?
text:
The tanker market of the end of 2017 and the beginning of 2018 will probably be remembered as one of the worst in recent history. The fact that the tanker market of the 1980s was much worse (and probably lasted longer) is of little consolation to shipowners experiencing earnings that regularly do not cover vessel operating expenses, let alone corporate overhead and financing costs. Within the tanker markets, the product carriers appear to be doing slightly better than crude carriers, but even in those markets there is little to write home about.
The reason for the poor rates across the board is straightforward: there are too many ships. The combined age profile of all the main tanker segments shows that new tanker deliveries slowed considerably in the period 2013-2015, setting the stage for a healthy tanker market in 2015. However, the subsequent pickup in deliveries in 2016 and 2017 put tanker rates under pressure again. The current tanker orderbook shows a continued high level of deliveries scheduled for 2018, with a distinct drop-off in 2019 (although vessels can still be ordered for late 2019 delivery). In line with general market consensus, this suggests that 2018 will continue to be a challenging year. Shipowners can help the market and maybe accelerate a recovery by scrapping older tankers as special surveys come due and by not immediately ordering replacement vessels, despite attractive shipyard prices.
The other side of the equation is oil and tanker demand. The OPEC/Non-OPEC production cutbacks have hurt the tanker market, especially since Middle East producers continue to target market share in the growing Asian markets. OPEC is primarily cutting back on the long-haul trades to Europe and the U.S. as demand growth in the OECD countries in the Atlantic Basin is limited and domestic oil production (in particular shale oil from the U.S.) is increasing rapidly. OPEC also hopes that their cutbacks will reduce the highly visible inventory levels in these markets and provide support to oil prices.
Summarizing the state of the crude tanker markets, one could say that we are at a critical juncture in the market: if scrapping picks up and new orders remain subdued, we set the stage for a tanker market recovery, the timing of which will primarily be driven by OPEC's production decisions (at least for the VLCC and Suezmax markets).

Few oil publications are followed as closely as the Weekly Petroleum Status Report, published every Wednesday morning by the U.S. Energy Information Administration. It gives a detailed account of weekly U.S. petroleum balances, including domestic oil production, imports, exports and movements in crude oil and petroleum product inventories. Prices move as a result of this report, especially when the movements are unexpected (which happens on a regular basis). This week was one of those weeks: counter to what most analysts expected, U.S. crude inventories fell and oil prices jumped. There are a lot of moving parts that go into these balances and some are influencing (or influenced by) the tanker market.

Another potential source of future oil supplies from the U.S. is the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR). Deep underground storage caverns along the Texas and Louisiana Gulf Coast have the capacity to hold 727 million barrels of crude oil. Owned by the U.S. Government, it is the largest emergency supply of crude oil in the world. The SPR currently holds around 665 million barrels of crude oil. One of the SPR's core missions is to hold enough oil stocks to meet the requirement of the International Energy Agency (IEA) to maintain at least 90 days of net import protection. The rapid increase of domestic production in the U.S. has significantly reduced net imports of crude oil and petroleum products into the United States. Since 2005, the volume of oil stored in the SPR had been mostly stable at around 700 million barrels, but that has started to change. Since March of last year, the volume of oil stored in the SPR has been gradually reduced by 30 million barrels (from 695 million barrels in March 2017 to 665 million barrels currently). Further declines are expected over the next 10 years. Several bills enacted under the Obama presidency in 2015 and 2016 collectively call for the sale of 149 million barrels in U.S. government fiscal years (FY) 2017 through 2025. Recent legislation by the Trump administration has directed the sale of an additional 100 million barrels of oil from the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve in FY 2022 through 2027. Based on the combination of these legislated sales established in multiple acts of Congress, the SPR could decline by about 40% in the coming decade while still meeting requirements for petroleum import coverage. The SPR could decline from 695 million barrels at the start of 2017 to about 410 million barrels at the start of 2028.
The combination of these changes in the U.S. oil markets, i.e. higher production, more exports, lower imports and sales from the SPR make it more difficult to predict the movements in commercial crude oil stocks. The reduction in imports have made the U.S. a less important discharge area for crude oil tankers, but the rapid increase in crude exports (following the lifting of the export ban) has transformed the U.S. Gulf into a key export area.

section_path: The potential impact of geopolitics has increased
section_path_text: The potential impact of geopolitics has increased
text:
Back in 2014, when oil prices were well above $100 per barrel, analysts regularly talked about a geopolitical "risk premium" to explain the high oil prices. The theory is that geopolitical tensions, in particular those in oil producing countries or regions, can raise fears of supply shortages and push oil prices higher. However, since the oil price collapse in 2014, the market has been awash in oil and the impact of geopolitical events on the oil markets has been muted. This may be about to change. More than a year after OPEC and select non-OPEC countries decided to cut back production and exports, global oil markets are rebalancing (despite runaway growth in U.S. production) and the synchronized growth in the major world economies has pushed up demand for oil and oil products. At the same time, geopolitical tensions in the world have increased. In today's weekly opinion, we will review some of the key supply risks facing the oil markets and the impact potential disruptions may have on the tanker market.
A review of the key OPEC and non-OPEC producers that agreed to curtail production shows that some participants are better (or more committed) to trimming output than others. Some individual production cutbacks are also more the result of domestic problems rather than commitment to OPEC policy. The countries that currently pose the most significant risk to global oil supplies are Venezuela, Iran and Iraq. Less risky, but still worth monitoring are Libya and Nigeria.
Venezuela has an OPEC production quota of 1.97 million barrels per day (mb/d). In January 2017, Venezuela produced 1.61 mb/d, 360,000 b/d below its allocation and almost 500,000 b/d less than its output in December 2016, the last month before the OPEC cuts became effective. The reduction in Venezuelan output has nothing to do with the OPEC agreement, but is entirely due to domestic production problems. Analysts expect that Venezuelan production will decline by another 400- 600,000 b/d this year. Venezuela's troubled economy and tense political climate, which has only been exacerbated by U.S. sanctions, make a recovery in the near term very unlikely.
Iranian production has been fairly stable in recent months. After the sanctions were lifted in 2016, Iranian production quickly recovered from 2.9 mb/d (Dec. 2015) to 3.8 mb/d (the average of 2017).

section_path_text: The latest IEA forecast is bullish on tanker trade
text:
The overall tone of "Oil 2018", the latest IEA annual forecast of global oil demand, supply, refining and trade is fairly positive and many of the specific elements that are discussed in the report are rather bullish for the tanker market. A combination of robust global demand growth, refining capacity expansion and changes in tradeflows could help the recovery in the tanker market. Even the IMO mandated changes in marine fuel specifications that will come into effect in 2020 could have a silver lining for the tanker market.
The IEA expects solid increases in oil demand based on a strong world economy. Outside of Europe, whose oil demand is expected to start declining again after 2018, all major regions in the world will show demand growth according to the IEA. Between 2017 and 2023, global oil demand will expand by 6.9 million barrels per day (mb/d). The Asia Pacific region will be by far the fastest growing region, followed by the Middle East. Africa and the Americas will expand at a slower pace. Within Asia, China and India will drive this growth and these countries, who represent 50% of global demand growth in the period through 2023, are both heavily dependent on imports. Demand growth in the Pacific Basin will stimulate long-haul tanker demand, especially since most of the oil production growth is happening in the Atlantic Basin. We will discuss this in more detail below.
The oil production growth in the United States is a bullish factor. The IEA forecasts that more than half of the growth in the world's production capacity between 2018 and 2023 (3.7 mb/d out of 6.4 mb/d) will come from the U.S. Canada, Brazil and Norway are also expanding their production. A lot of different factors will drive how this will play out in terms of tradeflows, but the IEA describes a plausible scenario that would lead to expanding U.S. crude oil exports to Europe and Asia. The expectation is that almost all the incremental oil that will be produced in Canada (about 1 mb/d over five years) will be exported (via pipeline and/or rail) to the U.S. because Canadian producers are facing an uphill battle getting export pipelines to either the east or west coast of their country approved. The increased imports of the heavy Canadian crudes will satisfy most of the incremental demand from refiners in the U.S. Gulf area.

This will create both a deficit of middle distillates and a surplus of high-sulphur fuel oil. Refiners will try to address this by using more light and low-sulphur crudes such as U.S. LTO. This will be particularly attractive for European refiners, which are already short middle distillates.
Then there is the refined product side of the market. The IEA expects the Middle East to lead in incremental refined product exports, followed by the U.S. and China. The IMO change will also lead to more diesel imports into the bunkering hub of Singapore.
Most of the changes discussed above are adding to ton-mile demand. This will help balance the tanker market over time and provide some much- needed support for owners.

The expression "history repeats itself" is very appropriate in the shipping markets. Seasonality and market cycles usually repeat themselves with a certain predictability. Earlier this week, one of my colleagues pointed out that so far in 2018 VLCC rates are trending very similar to 2013. Rates have been very disappointing this year with (seemingly) little improvement on the horizon. We thought it would be interesting to look back five years and see where 2018 may be similar to 2013 and where it could be different. After all, 2013 ended on a high note, with VLCC rates in November/December of that year averaging well over $50,000 per day, a far cry from the $13,000/day average for the other 10 months of the year. Could this year have a similar happy ending?
Let's first compare the fleet and the orderbook. In January 2013, there were 82 VLCC's on order for delivery through 2015. Based on a fleet of 612 vessels at the time, this represented 13.4% of the fleet. The VLCC fleet has grown significantly over the last five years. As per January 1 st of 2018, the VLCC fleet stood at 735 vessels (a net growth of 123 units or 20%). However, the relative statistics are similar: the current orderbook is 92 vessels, or 12.5% of the fleet (a slightly lower proportion than in 2013). We know rates have been similar so far this year, but how do newbuilding and secondhand prices compare to the prices half a decade ago? Newbuilding prices for VLCCs are about 10% lower now than they were in 2013 ($83 versus $92 million), but secondhand prices are slightly higher. section_path_text: U.S. refined product exports continue to grow
text:
The rapid growth of U.S. crude oil production and (more recently) the rise of crude oil exports from the U.S. Gulf have grabbed all the headlines. However, the U.S. still produces and exports more refined products than crude and this trade continues to grow. In a report that came out this week the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) noted that U.S. exports of petroleum products grew by 555,000 barrels per day (b/d) in 2017 to reach 5.2 million b/d. This was a 12% increase over 2016. Not as high as the 89% increase in crude oil exports, but still a healthy growth rate. Within the group of petroleum products, there is a wide discrepancy in growth rates between the different commodities, various export destinations and, in the case of seaborne exports, what kind of vessel is used for the movement. In today's Opinion, we will elaborate on these developments to determine the impact of these U.S. exports on the international product tanker market.
The refining industry in the U.S. continues to expand, assisted by strong product demand, both domestic and international. From 2016 to 2017, refining output in the U.S. grew by 379,000 b/d (+2.3%) to reach 19,893 kb/d. The operating capacity of the U.S. refiners barely changed, but the utilization rate went up from 89.7% in 2016 to 91% in 2017. As domestic demand in the U.S. has not changed significantly in recent years, most of the additional product output is being exported. We expect that U.S. refiners will maintain their competitive edge in world market based on growing domestic crude supplies and ample cheap natural gas to power their facilities. Earlier this month ExxonMobil announced that they expect to add 400,000 b/d of capacity to their Gulf Coast refineries by 2025.
A review of the U.S. petroleum product exports since 2000 (see chart) shows that export volumes started to take off a little more than 10 years ago, primarily driven by middle distillates (diesel). Middle distillates are still the largest export product. In 2017, the U.S. exported 1.4 million b/d according to the EIA, 17% more than the 2016 volumes.

section_path: Will Iranian Sanctions Make a Comeback?
section_path_text: Will Iranian Sanctions Make a Comeback?
text:
For most of this decade, Iranian oil production and exports have been reduced due to international sanctions, imposed as a result of of its nuclear ambitions and because of humanitarian concerns. In July 2015, the P5+1 (China, France, , Russia, the U.K the U.S and Germany.) reached an agreement (JCPOA) with Iran on its nuclear capabilities in return for sanctions relief. The implementation phase of the sanctions relief started in January 2016. President Trump has for a long time expressed his dissatisfaction with the agreement and in October 2017 announced that he would not recertify the agreement. The next deadline to extend the sanctions waiver is May 12, 2018, and at this point the Trump administration may announce that the U.S. will snap back its sanctions on Iran. In this opinion we will review Iran's recent crude production and exports and discuss the possible impact of renewed sanctions on the tanker market.
In December 2015, before sanctions relief went into effect, Iran produced 2.91 Million barrels per day (Mb/d) of crude oil. Iran managed to increase production faster than many analysts expected and by December 2016, production had increased to 3.77 MB/d. Production growth has stabilized since, and currently the IEA estimates production at around 3.8 Mb/d.
Based on Lloyd's List Intelligence data, Iran has exported an average of 2.2 Mb/d of crude oil over the last 6 months. China is the single largest importer with about 0.6 Mb/d and as the 2 nd graph indicates, imports have remained largely constant, even after the sanctions were lifted. Other large Asian importers are India, Japan and Korea. Combined with China, these countries account for about 65% of the total seaborne exports. Since the lifting of sanctions, countries in the Mediterranean, especially Turkey, Italy and Greece have re- emerged into large importers of Iranian crude.
Given the high proportion of Far Eastern buyers, VLCC's represent the main vessel class for Iranian exports, about 55% of the total. Suezmaxes are used for about 35% of the total exports, and logically dominate the Mediterranean trades and about half the volumes to India also move on Suezmax tankers.

Replacement barrels for Japan and Korea would mostly be sourced from other Middle Eastern countries, reducing the impact on the VLCC market. Lost European barrels might be replaced by a combination of Middle Eastern crude and short haul Russian barrels from the Baltic and the Black Sea, resulting in a minor negative impact. section_title: Will pipeline constraints hold back U.S. crude exports?
section_path: Will pipeline constraints hold back U.S. crude exports?
section_path_text: Will pipeline constraints hold back U.S. crude exports?
text:
For any product or commodity to be successful in the marketplace, it is important that it can be produced for a competitive price and in sufficient volumes and is delivered to customers on a timely basis. These rules apply to crude oil as well. In the United States, the rapid growth in light tight oil (LTO) production, in particular from the Permian Basin in Texas, has created some logistical challenges that are currently being addressed. On the one hand expanded production requires more pipelines to expand the takeaway capacity out of the region. On the other hand, to facilitate more exports, midstream operators are also investing in crude oil terminals, storage facilities and connecting pipelines. The question is: will the infrastructure expansion be ready in time to accommodate the expected growth in oil production and exports?
There are a lot of moving parts in the U.S. crude oil production, transportation and export puzzle. In recent years, West Texas, in particular the Permian Basin has been the largest source of production growth in the United States. Total onshore production of crude and condensate in Texas amounted to 4.0 mb/d in 2017, up 640 kb/d from the end of 2015. According to the IEA, some 2.8 million b/d of new pipeline capacity is expected to be built between 2018 and 2020. This new capacity is critical to handle the rapidly increasing LTO production. At the end of 2017, production and exports were closely matched and the expectation is that with rising LTO production tight pipeline capacity will turn into a deficit in the second half of 2018 and this gap could widen until mid-2019. From 2020 onward pipeline capacity is expected to be more than adequate to satisfy production and exports. Almost every U.S. midstream company is involved in one or more pipeline projects in the Permian and Eagle Ford basins. If all projects are built, takeaway capacity will more than double to reach 5.8 mb/d by the end of 2020 (see figure 1). A lot of the planned projects for 2018 and early 2019 are expansions of existing pipelines, while significant new construction will start to come online in 2019 & 2020. The biggest new pipelines are the 550,000 b/d EPIC pipeline (due 3Q19) and the South Texas Gateway (600,000 b/d due 1Q20).

text:
During the most recent session of its Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC), which took place from April 9 th to 13 th in London, the International Maritime Organization (IMO) adopted an initial strategy to reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from international shipping (the "GHG Strategy"). The headline target of the agreement is to reduce the total annual GHG emissions from international shipping by at least 50% by 2050 (32 years from now) compared to 2008. According to the IMO, which is the agency of the United Nations responsible for regulating shipping, "The strategy includes a specific reference to a pathway of CO2 emissions reduction consistent with the Paris Agreement temperature goals. While some member states and lobby groups would have preferred a commitment to even higher reductions, it appears that the IMO has reached a compromise that is ambitious enough to avoid unilateral regulations by member states, like the EU. The impact of the GHG Strategy on the shipping industry (shipowners and shipyards) will be profound. The effect of the introduction of ballast water treatment systems and the reduction in sulphur content of bunker fuels pales in comparison to the impact that the implementation of these rules will have on our industry.
Greenhouse gases, which scientists started linking to global warming in the 1960s and '70s, were first discussed by the United Nations (UN) in 1988. It became a key topic in 1992, during the "Earth Summit" in Rio de Janeiro, and in 1997, the Kyoto Protocol adopted binding targets for 37 industrialized countries and the European community to reduce GHG emissions. After Kyoto, the IMO started to pay attention to GHG emissions from ships and the First IMO GHG Study published in 2000, estimated that international shipping contributed about 1.8% of the world total anthropogenic (originating in human activity) CO2 emissions in 1996. The Second IMO GHG Study from 2009, estimated shipping's contribution for 2007 to be 2.8%. The third (most recent) study, done in 2014, estimated international shipping to emit 2.3% of global CO2 in 2012 (see table).
In 2016, the IMO mandated that ships of 5,000 gross tonnage and above will have to collect consumption data for each type of fuel they use.

So, how will the industry go about meeting the IMOs aggressive GHG reduction targets? There are two obvious avenues: (1) improving ship efficiency, and/or (2) switching to low (or zero) carbon fuels. Given these ambitious goals, the industry will need to aggressively pursue both avenues.
Since 2011, the MEPC has started to focus on guidelines to improve ship energy efficiency as a way to reduce GHG emissions. In July of that year, the IMO mandated the Energy Efficiency Design Index (EEDI) for new ships and the Ship Energy Efficiency Management Plan (SEEMP) for all ships. The EEDI requires a minimum energy efficiency level per capacity mile, and this level is to be tightened incrementally every five years. We are currently in phase 1 (10% reduction). Phase 2 (20% reduction) will go into effect in 2020 and EEDI phase 3, provisionally scheduled for 2025 will force all vessels built after that year to be 30% more efficient than the current fleet. It is important to note that the calculation of EEDI values is complex and varies by ship type, so the information above is necessarily simplified. SEEMP is an operational measure that establishes a mechanism to improve the energy efficiency of a ship in a cost-effective manner. It encourages shipping companies to manage ship and fleet efficiency performance over time and to incorporate best practices for fuel efficient ship operation.
The technology of Zero Emission Vessels (ZEVs) is developing rapidly. A 2017 study by LR and University Maritime Advisory Services (UMAS) identified several options, including biofuels, fuel cells, batteries and synthetic fuels (hydrogen and ammonia). However, none of these options are expected to be competitive compared to conventional fuels by within the next 10-15 years unless a significant carbon tax was applied.
At the moment, as the LR/UMAS correctly points out, there does not seem to be a "silver bullet" to replace fossil fuels in shipping. A combination of available options seems to be the way to go. There is still time, but the challenges facing the industry are so big that it we need to start addressing it sooner rather than later.

text:
While the tanker market has remained in the doldrums so far this year, demolition has picked up substantially. That makes sense. That is what we expect to happen when the freight markets turn down for an extended period of time. Another thing that we expect under these circumstances is a decline in newbuilding orders. When tanker rates are hovering around (and sometimes well below) operating expenses, who would want to (or can afford to) build expensive new vessels? Surprisingly, newbuilding orders are continuing despite low rates, stretched balance sheets and a general lack of financing? What is going on?
In the first four months of 2018, tanker rates have been depressed. Product carriers, in particular MRs, have fared better than crude oil tankers and across both markets, the largest vessels (VLCCs in crude and LR2s in products) are underperforming the most. VLCCs are suffering from a steady influx of new tonnage and subdued demand growth due to the continuing OPEC production cuts. Rising U.S. domestic production also has cut into long haul tanker demand as the refiners are using more domestic crude. In the face of rising pipeline imports from Canada, seaborne U.S. crude oil imports from the Middle East have declined disproportionately. Increased crude oil exports from the U.S. Gulf have been able to mitigate these developments to some extent, but not completely. The short-term outlook for the tanker market remains negative as OPEC has signaled a continued commitment to production cuts and newbuildings continue to be delivered at a steady clip. As of April 1, 9 VLCCs, 14 Suezmaxes, 16 Aframaxes/LR2s, 6 Panamaxes/LR1s and 12 MRs have been delivered, a total of 57 vessels. Another 200 vessels are scheduled for delivery over the remainder of this year, including 46 VLCCs and 33 Suezmaxes. So, why do owners continue to order new vessels?

Since November 2017, 31 VLCCs have been ordered. One third of the total (11 vessels) were ordered by various Chinese entities. Not surprisingly these vessels were all ordered at Chinese shipyards (Dalian and Jinhai).

Since November 2017, 31 VLCCs have been ordered. One third of the total (11 vessels) were ordered by various Chinese entities. All of these companies, most of them family owned, have a long shipping tradition. Some are building one or two vessels while others are making a more significant commitment to the industry. All the orders from the Greek owners (9 total from November 2017 - March 2018) were placed at shipyards in Korea. Some of the Greek orders are driven by fleet replacement in combination Korean owners placed several other orders at Korean yards. Of the remaining orders, three are from Japanese owners at - you guessed it - a Japanese shipyard.
As is almost always the case in shipping, the reasoning of the owners to order these vessels makes sense from their (individual) perspective. They intend to replace an ageing fleet, take advantage of historically low newbuilding prices and/or they want to position themselves for future demand growth and higher freight rates. The problem arises if too many owners have the same ideas at the same time: the expected market improvements never materialize. We may not be at that stage yet, but the ingredients are there: many owners are positive about the medium-term outlook for the tanker market and enough of them have the financial resources to make a down payment on one or more newbuildings.
The pickup in scrapping is encouraging and increased demolition will obviously reduce the impact of the newbuilding deliveries this year and next. However, as long as the market remains significantly oversupplied, tanker owners would benefit from a pause in tanker contracting. Against that backdrop, recent reports that some investment funds are eyeing speculative asset play because of low newbuilding prices offered by Chinese and Korean yards are troublesome. That is not what the tanker market needs.

In this weeks' Tanker Opinion, we will try to analyze what the net impact on the tanker market has been of this rapid increase in U.S. production and exports.

So, the reduction in seaborne crude oil imports in the U.S. was very significant from 2005 to 2015. However, After the export ban was lifted, the economics for crude oil imports changed dramatically.

section_title: Oil prices are rising as the summer driving season starts
section_path: Oil prices are rising as the summer driving season starts
section_path_text: Oil prices are rising as the summer driving season starts
text:
Memorial Day weekend marks the beginning of the "summer driving season" in the U.S. In addition to the traditional burgers and hot dogs on the grill, gasoline prices typically start sizzling as well. There is generally a seasonal uptick in gasoline demand and prices, for a variety of reasons. Although improved cars, all- weather tires and better roads mean that people can easily travel much of the year, traditionally, still more people hit the road in the summer. School vacations exacerbate this trend. The difference between peak gasoline demand in the summer and the low point of the year, which is generally in January, is about 1 million barrels per day, according to the EIA (see figure 1). This trend has not materially changed over the years and the initial indications are that 2018 will follow the same pattern.
The impact of the summer driving season on the tanker market has diminished somewhat over the years. Nationwide, the U.S. has abundant refining capacity and ample gasoline inventories, so, barring any unforeseen events, the market should be well supplied. However, there are significant regional differences in the country because of regional supply and demand balances, gasoline specification requirements and taxes. U.S. Petroleum Administration for Defense District no. 1 (PADD1), the U.S. East Coast, for example, still imports significant quantities of gasoline (mostly gasoline blending components), with imports in the summer averaging more than double the movements in the winter. So far in 2018, weekly volumes have ranged from 300-350,000 barrels per day (b/d) in January to 650-700,000 b/d in May. Imports in the June-August period are expected to be even higher. Almost half of the PADD1 imports are short- haul moves from Canada, while various countries in Europe (including Russia) account for most of the remaining volumes. Import volumes into PADD3 and PADD5 are much lower (<100,000 b/d during peak periods), but they display the same seasonal pattern: low in the winter, high in the summer.
Since 2011, the United States has been a net exporter of petroleum products and gasoline has been a significant contributor to the growing product export trade. In 2017, the U.S. exported 821,000 b/d of Gasoline, 747,000 b/d (90%) of which was finished motor gasoline, the remainder was blending components.

section_path: Canadian and U.S. pipelines are a study in contrasts
section_path_text: Canadian and U.S. pipelines are a study in contrasts
text:
This week, the Canadian federal government announced that they are buying the Trans Mountain pipeline system and its expansion project from current owner Kinder Morgan for C$4.5 billion. The expansion itself (if it goes ahead) is expected to cost an additional C$7.4 billion. It is the latest chapter in a story that has taken many twists and turns. At this moment, the Trans Mountain system expansion project (TMEP) has received a lifeline from the Canadian government, which became necessary after Kinder Morgan strongly considered pulling out of the project. The Trans Mountain pipeline is the only Canadian pipeline that moves domestic crude to the country's coastline for exports. While its capacity is 300,000 b/d, some 74% (221,000 b/d) of the throughput of the Trans Mountain pipeline is allocated to refineries with connections in British Columbia and Washington State. Only about 80,000 b/d is allocated to the Westridge Terminal in Burnaby, British Columbia (near Vancouver). This is enough to load one Aframax (the maximum vessel size for this facility) per week. This is only a trickle when compared to Canada's oil production which, in March 2018, held steady near a record 5.2 million b/d (IEA). Even if the Trans Mountain expansion goes ahead, tanker exports will remain relatively small.
It was not always expected to be that way. In late 2014/early 2015, the outlook for Canadian production and exports was rosy. Several export pipelines were planned and analysts (including us) were forecasting a significant change in tanker trade flows in the 2017-2018 time-frame. An overview of the North American pipeline proposals updated by the Canadian Association of Petroleum Producers (CAPP) in September 2014, showed Keystone XL (+830,000 b/d), Energy East (+1,100,000 b/d), Northern Gateway (+525,000 b/d) and the Trans Mountain Expansion (+590,000 b/d). These projects combined represented more than 3 million b/d of additional pipeline export capacity for Canadian oil producers, all to be completed before 2019. Here we are in the middle of 2018 and none of this new capacity has been built. Northern Gateway and Energy East have been cancelled altogether, the Keystone XL is still mired in legal problems (even though the Trump administration fast-tracked the State Department approval) and the Trans Mountain Expansion is on life-support.

section_path: The tanker market is hoping for production increases
section_path_text: The tanker market is hoping for production increases
text:
Some OPEC meetings are more important than others and the one coming up on June 22 is shaping up to be one of the more significant gatherings of the group of oil exporting countries as they will discuss whether to maintain their production cuts or increase production. Since the current production restrictions went into effect in January 2017, oil prices have increased from $55 to $80 per barrel for Brent. Commercial inventories in the United States have come down 100 million barrels from a peak of 534 million in April 2017 to around 436 million barrels in the first week of June 2018. While these two elements seem to indicate that the OPEC cuts have achieved their objective, it remains highly uncertain what OPEC (and non-OPEC participants, like Russia) will ultimately decide to do. The tanker market is holding its collective breath. A meaningful increase in long-haul flows from some of the key OPEC exporters would go a long way in turning the (crude) tanker market around, especially since it will impact the physical market as well as provide a boost to the all-important market psychology.
While the production cutbacks and resulting oil price increases seem to have turned the finances around for the OPEC countries, some members are benefiting more than others. Chart 1 shows the annual changes in the aggregate value of the oil exports for each of the OPEC countries from 2014 - 2017. It clearly shows the decline in revenues in 2015 after the oil price collapsed in the second half of 2014. Revenues declined on average by 45%! As the largest OPEC producer and exporter, Saudi Arabia suffered the most. The value of the Kingdom's petroleum exports dropped from $284 billion in 2014 to $153 billion in 2015. It was no surprise that OPEC decided in 2016 that they needed to curtail production. This led to a significant recovery in price which boosted the revenues for all OPEC members. However, the total value of exports remains significantly below the 2013/2014 numbers.
The paths of the different OPEC members may diverge from here. Sticking to the production agreement may lead to higher oil prices and this will further improve OPEC's finances. However, the world economy is not immune to higher oil prices and pressure from the U.S. on OPEC is building to increase production.

The worst case would be a decision later this month to do nothing, i.e. continue the production cuts. This will lead to rising prices as problems in Venezuela continue to mount and many Iranian buyers gradually start to reduce their purchases to avoid U.S. sanctions. As we move closer to the November cutoff, Iranian exports may decline further. A tightening oil market in combination with rising geopolitical tension could push oil prices to levels where it starts to impact global demand. Rising U.S. oil production is a positive for global oil balances, but, due to a lack of pipeline capacity, U.S. shale producers are facing increasing problems getting their product to (export) markets.

section_title: Can growing ton-mile demand turn the market?
section_path: Can growing ton-mile demand turn the market?
section_path_text: Can growing ton-mile demand turn the market?
text:
The freight markets for 2018 have so far been disappointing for crude oil tankers. For the VLCC market, the supply-demand balance and the resulting freight rates are predominantly driven by OPEC production and exports. Suezmaxes and Aframaxes typically have more diverse trading patterns. This week we will take a look at what may be behind the disappointing returns for these medium sized crude oil tankers.
Suezmaxes have suffered more than most other segments, as some of their traditional markets have declined dramatically in recent years. However, examining the Suezmax trades over recent years shows that these ships have been effective in finding alternative employment. It might be a surprise to some readers that, over the first four months of this year, ton-mile demand for Suezmax tankers actually increased by 7% compared to the prior year as Suezmaxes performed on average 27.5 more voyages per month. The strongest growth was on the Middle East to India route, which increased from an average of 28 cargoes per month in 2017 to 39 this year (Jan-Apr). A large part of the growth was due to increased Iranian exports to India, which could be threatened in the second half of the year by the reinstatement of U.S. sanctions on Iran. Suezmax tankers also managed to recapture some market share in West Africa from VLCCs as less West African crude moved to Asia. Europe bought more West African crude, resulting in an increase of about 10 monthly voyages to NW Europe and the Mediterranean. Suezmaxes also benefited from the growing exports from the U.S. Gulf, mainly for short and medium haul voyages to Canada (+2.8 voy/m) and Europe (+4.3 voy/m).
Suezmax trades were negatively affected by the dispute over oil exports between the Kurds in Northern Iraq and the Iraqi government after the vote for independence in September 2017. Suezmax voyages from Ceyhan declined from 12 voyages per month in early 2017 to just 3.5 in 2018.
While the demand side was overall positive for Suezmax tankers, the supply side spelled trouble: over the last 12 months, the Suezmax fleet increased by 39 ships, equivalent to 7%, thereby offsetting the growth in demand.
For Aframax tankers the situation is mixed.

section_title: Will a trade war hurt the tanker market?
section_path: Will a trade war hurt the tanker market?
section_path_text: Will a trade war hurt the tanker market?
text:
As part of the ongoing effort by the U.S. administration to negotiate improved trade arrangements with China, the U.S has imposed tariffs on steel and aluminum imports and has threatened additional tariffs on other products. China is planning to retaliate with tariffs on U.S. products. The initial Chinese list of tariffs focused on agricultural and other products, but excluded oil and gas. However, recent reports suggest that China is considering 25% tariffs on imports of U.S. crude oil. Such tariffs would make U.S. crude less competitive against other potential sources of crude. This week we will look at what this could mean for the tanker market.
Since the U.S. lifted the ban on crude oil exports in December 2015, U.S. crude oil production has increased from 9.2 Million barrels per day (Mb/d) to 10.5 Mb/d. According to the U.S. Energy Administration, exports have reached 1.54 Mb/d in the first quarter of 2018. Most of the production increase consists of very light crude from shale fields which is not ideal for domestic refineries which were traditionally configured to run heavier (and cheaper) grades and a significant share of it is exported.
Over the last twelve months China has developed into the second largest crude oil buyer of U.S. crude with imports of 358 Kb/d in 2018, just behind Canada which imported 364 Kb/d. China accounts for more than half of the total volume of U.S. crude that is shipped to Asia. Other large Asian importers include Korea (110 Kb/d), Taiwan (75 Kb/d) and India (53 Kb/d).
Exports from the U.S. Gulf to Asia are important for tanker demand due to the long distance: The trip from the U.S. Gulf to China is about 10,300 nautical miles compared to a traditional voyage from the AG to China of about 5,900 miles. Additionally, due to the shallow draft and other constraints of ports in the U.S. Gulf, VLCCs are loaded using reverse lightering using smaller tankers. As a result, the U.S. Gulf to Asia trade provides employment for VLCCs and for Aframax tankers (and occasionally Panamax tankers) used for lightering.
Analysts believe that China could replace the U.S. imports with alternative crude sources, most likely from Saudi Arabia, Russia and possibly the North Sea.

It is questionable whether other Asian buyers will be able to absorb the Chinese volumes and it is more likely that Europe would buy the bulk of the additional volumes if the price is attractive.

If these cargoes are eliminated, the VLCC market will notice, especially if most of China's replacement barrels come from the Middle East and Russia. On the other hand, the Aframax and Suezmax markets will likely benefit from additional demand from Europe. Reverse lightering would be affected by reduced VLCC exports from the U.S. Gulf. 5-6 VLCC cargoes require about 20- 24 lightering voyages per month, but this would likely be more than offset by additional transatlantic employment. The question is which European imports will be displaced by U.S. exports; Russia, the Middle East?
There is still hope that all the threats of tariffs are just negotiating tactics and that very little of these tariffs are actually implemented or that they are in effect for only a short time. Until this all settles down, it is wise for the tanker industry to keep an eye on the tariff situation.

section_title: What if U.S. sanctions are reducing Iran exports close to zero?
section_path: What if U.S. sanctions are reducing Iran exports close to zero?
section_path_text: What if U.S. sanctions are reducing Iran exports close to zero?
text:
Most analysts, including ourselves in our Weekly Opinion of May 11 (" Iran Sanctions Snap Back "), expected the reduction in Iranian export to be gradual and limited. We thought the reduction could eventually reach 500-600,000 b/d (from an average of 2.6 mb/d in 2018 YTD down to 2.0 - 2.1 mb/d). However, an alternative scenario has been gaining traction, one where Iranian exports will be reduced even more than during the previous sanctions period. Reports from the U.S. State Department indicate that the Trump administration is not just looking for reductions in exports, like during the Obama administration. It aims to bring exports from Iran down to zero. While this may not be a realistic expectation, the United States is expected to use its considerable leverage to force rolling reductions in purchases from all buyers of Iranian crude and waivers are conditional on immediate cuts. The implications of deeper cuts into Iranian exports for the tanker market are uncertain; it depends to a large extent on which countries have the spare production capacity to make up the shortfall. The ultimate impact on tanker ton-mile demand hinges on the resulting changes in tradeflows.
Iran has ample experience in dealing with various kinds of sanctions and even if the U.S. applies maximum pressure on its trading partners, Iran will have various options to keep at least some of its exports flowing. As sanctions start to bite, it will try to lure buyers with discounts and extended payment terms. To circumvent U.S. banking restrictions, it could accept payment in other currencies or do barter deals. It has agreed to an oil swap with Iraq. Iran will also be using its own tanker fleet (one of the largest in the world) to move and store crude.
However, despite Iran's attempts to minimize the damage, early indications are not encouraging for them. Most international oil companies, especially those with meaningful U.S. operations, have already decided to steer clear from buying Iranian crude. U.S. allies like Japan and South Korea are under pressure to reduce their purchases. Turkey is also a significant buyer of Iranian oil and while they may resist pressure from the U.S. to cut back, they don't have a lot of room to increase their purchases either. The two countries that could take more Iranian crude are the two largest current buyers: India and China. Combined they imported about 1.4 million b/d over the past three months.

text:
For today's weekly opinion we decided to take a look at almost 5 years of crude oil trade data (2014 - 2018) to see if we can discern any interesting trends or developments. Are certain segments growing faster than others? How about shifts in export or import regions. Do we notice anything that we did not expect?
First, let's look at the overall crude oil and dirty product trade for the period 2014-2018. To make the earlier years com- parable with 2018, we look only at the first 6 months of the year. The data shows that the dirty tanker trade showed steady growth in the period 2014-2017, increasing almost 5% in the first 6 months of 2015 and still growing 2.2% and 3.3% in 2016 and 2017 respectively. However, in 2018 to date, the total dirty tanker trade (measured in Metric Tons) has been down 1.3% compared to the same period one year ago (TonMiles: -1.6%). The biggest decline in import demand, however, came from the United States (-15%). On the other hand, U.S. exports were one of the few bright spots in 2018 to date, with ton-mile demand more than double that of the same period last year. The long-haul trade to China was responsible for almost 60% of that increase.

section_title: Owners of older tankers face a dilemma
section_path: Owners of older tankers face a dilemma
section_path_text: Owners of older tankers face a dilemma
text:
Tanker scrapping has been on an upswing this year and in a recent interview, an executive from the demolition industry highlighted the main drivers for demolition in the tanker industry: (the outlook for) freight rates, current scrap prices and the demolition activity in other shipping segments are always a factor. Regulatory changes can also be a driver, particularly if there are significant rule changes on the horizon. The phase out of single hull vessels in the period 1999-2003, for example, pushed up demolition levels during that period. At the moment, the requirement to install ballast water treatment systems and the IMO 2020 sulphur cap for bunker fuels are factors that owners need to consider. Let's consider each of these drivers and see how they may impact scrapping in the coming years.
Without regulatory mandates, the freight market has been (and always will be) the main driver for ship owners facing the decision whether to scrap a vessel or continue to trade it. Not just the current market, but in particular the owner's expectations for future earnings. Tanker scrapping peaked in 1985 (at 10.5% of the existing fleet!) after many years of dismal earnings had sapped the confidence of tanker owners. Current spot earnings are also disappointing and are no doubt an important incentive for owners of older tonnage to consider selling their vessel for demolition. Relative to modern vessels, older tankers frequently have to offer discounted rates to keep employed and still face lower utilization, undermining their earnings even further. However, unlike in the mid-1980s, earnings have not been very bad for very long and most owners don't expect the market to stay depressed for a long period. Other factors must play a role as well.
How about scrap prices? Do they really play a significant role in an owner's decision? Historical data does not seem to bear that out. As the second chart shows, the two periods of elevated scrapping in 1992-1995 and 1999-2003 coincided with relatively low scrap prices. The high scrap prices of 2004-2008 occurred during the tanker super cycle, when scrapping was understandably low. Demolition picked up in 2009-2014, but that had more to do with the collapse in tanker rates after the global financial crisis than the relatively high scrap prices. In general, scrap prices are hard to predict for owners and most owners assume flat scrap prices going forward.

The potential costs of these mandates present a dilemma to a shipowner faced with a 3 rd or 4 th special survey. Take, for example the owner of a 2003 built VLCC who needs to decide whether to take the ship through the next two special surveys (15 and 17.5 years) with combined drydock costs of around $4-5 million. The installation of a ballast water treatment system could cost an additional $2-3 million. And then there is the matter of IMO 2020. Does the owner retro-fit a scrubber on his 15-year old vessel for $3 million? He may have to, if he wants to be able to effectively compete post 2020. Non- ECO vessels built in the early 2000s ago typically have a higher fuel consumption than modern tankers and if they need to burn expensive MGO starting in 2020, they may struggle to compete. A simple calculation indicates that a 15-year old VLCC would need to earn at least $16-17,000 per day to break even (i.e. return the investment). While that is entirely possible, the current freight market is about half that rate. Even if the owner has the cash to invest (banks may be reluctant to provide credit for this), he needs to be able to reserve a scrubber and schedule the installation to coincide with the upcoming drydock. Given the risks and uncertainties involved, one can also understand the owner who decides to scrap his ship instead.

section_path: Oil from the Kingdom flows through many chokepoints
section_path_text: Oil from the Kingdom flows through many chokepoints
text:
On Wednesday, July 25, Yemeni Houthi militia attacked two Saudi VLCCs after they passed through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a waterway that links the Gulf of Aden with the Red Sea. In response, Khalid al-Falih, Minister of Energy, Industry and Mineral Resources of the Kingdom and chairman of Saudi Aramco announced that Saudi Arabia would temporarily halt oil shipments through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait "until the situation becomes clearer and the maritime transit through Bab el- Mandeb is safe." Although it appears that the Houthi militia specifically target the merchant ships from nations supporting the Saudi led Coalition (SLC), there is always a risk of collateral damage or misidentification to all merchant traffic, including those not flagged to SLC states and Intertanko has urged their members transiting to this area to "utilize the Maritime Security Transit Corridor while remaining as far from the Yemen coast as navigationally safe." While we expect that the impact of the attack on the Bahri VLCCs will be both temporary and limited, it highlights some of the vulnerabilities for the largest OPEC producer as it depends on some of the biggest oil transit chokepoints for its crude oil and product exports.
This week, the focus is on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait which is located between Yemen, Djibouti and Eritrea. Based on the latest available data from the EIA, an estimated 4.8 million barrels per day (mb/d) of crude oil and refined petroleum products flowed through this waterway in 2016, 2.8 mb/d northbound and 2.0 mb/d southbound. Northbound movements are mostly crude oil for delivery to Saudi refineries on the Red Sea coast as well as crude deliveries to the Ain Sukhna terminal (for transport through the Sumed pipeline to Sidi Kerir) and last, but not least, direct shipments through the Suez Canal to the Mediterranean and Southern Europe. Southbound movements are predominantly products, a significant portion of which originate from Saudi export refineries on the country's west coast. Saudi Arabia has built more than 1.5 million b/d of refining capacity on the Red Sea coast, with another 400,000 b/d starting up later this year. Saudi Aramco has several ways to mitigate the impact of a long- term halt of shipments through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

section_title: U.S. refineries are churning out record product volumes
section_path: U.S. refineries are churning out record product volumes
section_path_text: U.S. refineries are churning out record product volumes
text:
In their latest weekly petroleum report, the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) noted that U.S. refineries are running at near-record levels. The four-week average of U.S. gross refinery inputs surpassed 18 million barrels per day (b/d) for the first time since the EIA started publishing this data in 1990. The last time refinery inputs approached 18 million b/d was in the week of August 25, 2017 (the week before Hurricane Harvey made landfall). The U.S. economy is currently running on all cylinders and GDP growth reached an annual rate of 4.1% in the second quarter. This is driving domestic product demand upwards, in particular for gasoline and distillate fuel oil, which (combined) count for almost 75% of refinery output in the United States. Exports of refined petroleum products are strong as well. Refined product exports (which includes LPGs and Pet Coke) have more than tripled over the last ten years, from an average of less than 1.8 million b/d in 2008 to 5.5 million b/d in 2018 year-to-date and the upward trend shows no sign of slowing down. Do these increases in activity have a noticeable impact on product tanker employment and rates?
Refinery inputs are seasonal and typically peak in the summer. As can be seen in the first chart, refinery maintenance increases in the spring when refiners are retooling their facilities to make summer gasoline. The same happens in the fall when they switch back to winter grades. The graph also shows that U.S. gross refinery inputs have been showing material growth in recent years. For many years, U.S. refining capacity expansions were limited to capacity creep, i.e. small increases in distillation capacity due to minor debottlenecking within existing facilities (often during maintenance turnarounds). However, since 2011, refinery capacity in the U.S. has increased by 862,000 b/d, partly due to the commissioning of four small new facilities (mostly condensate splitters) in Texas and one in North Dakota. Motiva significantly expanded its refinery in Port Arthur and Valero did the same with its Corpus Christi facility. Some idled capacity has been brought back on line as well. In short, U.S. refineries are in good shape, especially those on the Gulf Coast.

Projected deliveries for the remainder of this year and 2019 are less than in prior years and if ton-mile demand continues to grow, the outlook for the product market is rather positive. The shift towards low sulphur bunker fuels in 2020 represents a significant wildcard. This change may create dislocations in the marine fuels markets and therefore additional employment opportunities for product carriers, starting in the second half of 2019. U.S. crude oil exports have been on a tear since the crude oil export ban was lifted at the end of 2015. Initially, most of the export barrels were sold in Canada and Europe and the vessels of choice were Aframaxes and to a lesser extent Suezmaxes. The use of VLCCs was rare. However, since 2017, as U.S. production continued to grow, Asia has developed into an important destination for U.S. crude and VLCCs have become a more significant factor in the transportation mix. This was out of necessity. To be competitive in Asia on a landed cost basis, charterers need to use the largest tankers available. One VLCC can carry two million barrels, twice as much as a Suezmax and more than three times the volume of an Aframax. In 2018 VLCCs have become the vessel of choice for charterers. section_title: Key Asian producer wants to keep its oil in the country
section_path: Key Asian producer wants to keep its oil in the country
section_path_text: Key Asian producer wants to keep its oil in the country
text:
The financial crisis in Turkey has created sharp fluctuations in the value of the Turkish Lira and a general weakening of emerging market currencies over the last two weeks. One of the countries that is affected is Indonesia, a large oil producer in Asia. Indonesia, which faces a significant (and growing) current account deficit, has seen its currency weaken significantly this year. A little more than 20 years ago, Indonesia was one of the largest victims of the Asian Financial Crisis. President Joko Widodo, who faces re-election next year, does not want a repeat of that currency crisis, which ultimately led to the resignation of then-president Suharto (after 31 years in office). To support its currency, Indonesia, a former OPEC member, wants to curb its dollar denominated imports. Earlier this week, the minister of Energy and Mineral Resources directed state oil company Pertamina to buy all domestically produced crude oil, including the production from overseas companies like ExxonMobil and Chevron. It is still uncertain if and how this plan will be executed. However, Indonesia is a significant crude oil importer as well as exporter in Asia and in this Tanker Opinion we will discuss the potential implications for tradeflows in the region.
Indonesia is one of the world's oldest oil producers. In 1885, a Dutch tobacco planter discovered the first commercial quantities of oil in North Sumatra and founded a company that ultimately became the Royal Dutch/Shell Group. Indonesian oil production grew rapidly and peaked in 1977 at 1.7 million barrels per day. Starting in the early 1990s, production gradually declined and Indonesia's output dipped below 1 million b/d in 2007. Indonesia is the fourth most populous country in the world and in 2004 it became a net importer of oil as growing domestic demand overtook stagnant production. In recent years exports have struggled, while imports continued to increase.
Indonesia's export markets have traditionally been in Asia. Thailand, China and Singapore are the main destinations for its crude. The Par (ex-Chevron) refinery on Hawaii is also a regular recipient of Indonesian crude. Indonesia exports almost all its crude oil on Aframaxes, driven by the country's port restrictions and production infrastructure, a significant portion of which is offshore. Since Indonesia is a country consisting of more than 17,000 islands, most of the domestic distribution of crude oil also takes place with tankers. Aframaxes dominate the domestic trades as well.

Crude oil imports into Indonesia have grown over time and in recent years have exceeded exports. Most of Indonesia's crude oil imports originate from the Arabian Gulf and West Africa. The AG trade involves mostly VLCCs, although many of these are only part- cargoes. The vessels only discharge one third or one half of their cargo in Indonesia before they continue to their final destination. West African imports mostly arrive on Suezmaxes, while intra-Asian movements from countries like Malaysia and Australia are typically moved on Aframaxes.

The exports that are subject to long-term supply agreements will continue (although the contracts cannot be renewed), but all the spot cargoes will now be absorbed by the Indonesian state oil company. Pertamina has stated that this will cut its imports by 60%.
A 250,000 b/d reduction in availability of Indonesian crude means that regional buyers will have to source this crude elsewhere. Depending on the grade and quality of the crude, the most likely alternatives can be found in the Middle East or the Atlantic Basin (West Africa and the U.S.). For the tanker market this means more ton-miles and a move away from Aframaxes to VLCCs. At the same time, Indonesia will also need to import less. Historically, this would mean less long-haul crude from the Middle East on VLCCs although recently, Indonesia increased imports from short-haul producers in the Pacific Basin. Overall, Indonesia's new policy will likely have a limited impact on the tanker market although it could be slightly positive for VLCCs.

section_path: As expected, Panama Canal not a major factor for crude flows
section_path_text: As expected, Panama Canal not a major factor for crude flows
text:
On June 26 th , 2016 the container ship "COSCO Shipping Panama" was the first vessel that officially passed through the expanded Panama Canal. Since then, the trade has gradually expanded and has developed into a critical part of the maritime infrastructure. On July 29 th , 2018 the Panama Canal registered the transit of its 4,000 th Neopanamax vessel, when the LNG carrier Maria Energy made the passage from the Atlantic to the Pacific Ocean. In 2016 we wrote an Opinion (" To Fit or Retrofit ") indicating that oil tankers where initially only a small part of the ships transiting the Canal and that it would be interesting to see whether traders and oil companies would be able to develop trades that use the Canal. Now that the Canal has been open for a bit more than two years, we thought it would be interesting to review the current utilization of the Canal by Aframax and Suezmax tankers.
The capacity utilization of the Neopanamax locks has gradually increased. The design capacity of the locks was 12 transits per day but during the first few months the average number of transits was below 4 vessels per day. In July 2018, an average of 7.52 ships passed through the new expanded locks, the first month in which the average daily transits exceeded 7 vessels per day. The latest transit statistics provided by the canal authorities show that container ships make up almost half (49%) of the ships using the Neopanamax locks between October 2017 and June 2018. LPG (25%) and LNG (12%) tankers make up the vast majority of the remaining vessels passing through the Canal. LNG tanker transits were originally limited by daylight restrictions and an encounter restriction (two LNG vessels could not navigate Gatun Lake at the same time), but the canal authorities have gradually relaxed these restrictions. LNG transits are expected to increase further as more export capacity becomes available along the US Gulf and East Coast. So far, crude oil tankers make up only 3% of the total transits.
Since the opening of the Neopanamax locks, we have counted 92 transits of Aframax and Suezmax tankers. Many of the tankers have used the canal as a repositioning shortcut as more than half (53) of the transits where for oil tankers travelling in ballast.

In some cases, light loaded ships top up at the Trans Panama Pipeline (PTP) terminal before proceeding to the USWC. section_title: How much will shipping costs increase for charterers?
section_path: How much will shipping costs increase for charterers?
section_path_text: How much will shipping costs increase for charterers?
text:
So far, the discussion around the implementation of IMO's low sulphur bunker fuel mandate ("IMO 2020") has primarily centered around the choices that shipowners have available to them. Will they switch to low sulphur fuel oil, install scrubbers to enable them to continue to use high sulphur bunkers or explore alternative fuels like LNG? Much less has been written about how IMO 2020 will impact marine transportation costs and who will likely pay for it. Because there remains a lot of uncertainty around the pricing of alternative fuel options and the adoption of abatement technologies such as scrubbers, it is difficult to forecast the exact impact IMO 2020 will have on shipping costs, but based on our assumptions, we think the costs are significant and will (likely) increase transportation expenses for tanker charterers. Because ocean transportation will remain by far the cheapest (and sometimes the only) way to move commodities over long distances, we don't expect it to have a large impact on global transportation volumes.

section_title: Keeping An Eye On The Hurricanes
section_path: Keeping An Eye On The Hurricanes
section_path_text: Keeping An Eye On The Hurricanes
text:
Potential impact of tropical storms in the US Gulf is increasing This week, tropical storm Gordon, the first major weather event of the 2018 hurricane season, carved through the eastern Gulf of Mexico, making landfall just west of the Alabama-Mississippi border on Tuesday night. While this storm caused minimal property damage, it was a poignant reminder of the risks facing the significant (and growing) energy sector in the U.S. Gulf. One year ago, Hurricane Harvey, the most powerful storm to hit the U.S. in more than a decade, made landfall on the central Texas coast and severely disrupted oil production and refining operations in the region. More than 300,000 barrels per day (b/d) of offshore oil production was taken offline and an estimated 3 million b/d of refining capacity was shut down. We cannot predict how disruptive this year's hurricane season is going to be, but with the continued growth of the oil & gas infrastructure in the U.S. Gulf, any significant storm hitting the Gulf Coast increases the risk of disruption to the oil and tanker markets. Hurricanes are not an exclusively American or Atlantic Basin phenomenon. The Western Pacific Basin (where they call the most powerful storms typhoons rather than hurricanes) has had its share of tropical storms. This week, Japan was struck by typhoon Jebi, the worst storm to strike the country since 1993. China, Korea and the Philippines are also regularly hit by typhoons. However, no region in the world has such a large concentration of energy infrastructure in one place as the U.S. Gulf region. That is why storms that happen there have much more of an impact on the oil and tanker markets.
The first chart on this page shows the timing and impact on Caribbean tanker rates of some of the biggest hurricanes that hit the U.S. Gulf since January 2000. This first one is Ivan from September 2004 and the last one is Harvey from September 2017. As can be seen on the chart, many of these storms caused a major spike in Aframax rates in the Caribbean. In the weeks following Ivan, rates spiked from below $20,000/day to more than $70,000/day. The double whammy of Rita and Katrina in August/September 2005 had a similar impact (from $15,000/day to $68,000/day in a matter of weeks).

What are the main reasons for the freight market spikes that typically follow these hurricanes? While each hurricane is different, there are some common variables that play a role. Typically, shipowners and refiners can see a hurricane coming and have some time to prepare. Before a hurricane makes landfall, refiners will reduce runs and limit crude oil deliveries to the refinery. Shipowners want to stay out of harm's way and will fix their vessels to other destinations. Once the hurricane hits, affected refiners may further cut runs or stop operating altogether and ports will be closed with no vessels being able to enter or leave. Depending on the extent of the damage, refiners, ports, terminals and pipelines will need time to bring their operations back online. Even if the damage is limited, vessels will not be immediately available to load and/or discharge their cargo. Once the infrastructure is back online, many charterers will get back in the market to try to fix vessels to resupply their refineries. Chances are that many vessels have been fixed to other destinations and there is a shortage of prompt tonnage available. The competition for a limited number of vessels will quickly push up rates. This will eventually attract more tonnage back into the area and the market will rebalance and rates will come down again.
